R08-A-01: In a number of countries a newborn cannot simply be given whatever name the parents choose. A registrar may refuse a name that is judged offensive, that does not clearly indicate whether the bearer is male or female, that is spelt in a way the national orthography does not allow, or that does not appear on an official list. Defenders of such rules usually present them as a modest form of child protection. Parents, the argument runs, are fallible and sometimes vain; the child carries the name for a lifetime and had no say in choosing it; and the state, which already requires that children be schooled and vaccinated, may reasonably insist that they not be saddled with a label that will invite mockery. There is something to this. A name is not a private ornament but a tool that other people use, and a name that cannot be pronounced, written on a form or read out in a classroom without laughter does impose a cost on the person who bears it. Cases in which parents have tried to register a brand name, a string of numbers or an insult are real enough, and few people would object to a registrar declining them. If the rules went no further than this, they would hardly be worth arguing about. But they usually go much further, and the further they go, the less work the child-protection argument does. A rule that a name must indicate the bearer's sex protects no child from ridicule; it protects a social expectation. A rule that a name may use only the letters of the national alphabet does not shield the daughter of immigrant parents from mockery; if anything, it obliges her to carry an altered spelling of her grandmother's name, one that marks her at every roll call as someone whose family had to be corrected. An approved list, finally, protects children chiefly from novelty, and novelty is not a harm. Many names now regarded as solid and traditional were once eccentric inventions, and a register that had frozen the stock of names a century ago would have prevented most of them. What the stricter rules actually defend, then, is the stock of names itself, treated as a piece of national heritage that private choices might erode. That is a coherent aim, and some will think it a worthy one. It should, however, be argued for openly as cultural policy and weighed against the interest parents have in naming their children as their own traditions require, rather than smuggled in under the language of protecting the young. A state that wishes to guard children from cruel names needs a short list of what is forbidden, not a long list of what is allowed.
R08-A-02: The quarrel between those who lay down rules for English and those who merely record how it is spoken is usually staged as a contest between snobbery and science. On one side stand the guardians of usage, who object to split infinitives and sentence-final prepositions and who regard each new sense of an old word as a small act of vandalism. On the other stand the linguists, who point out that many of the rules are of recent and dubious origin, that admired writers have broken them for centuries, and that a grammar describing what speakers actually do is the only kind that deserves the name. Put this way, the linguists win easily, and in the universities, at least, they have been winning for a long time. Yet the victory is less complete than it appears, because it rests on a confusion about what a rule of usage is. The linguist is right that no rule of this kind is a law of the language in the way that, say, the order of article and noun is: speakers who break it are still perfectly understood, and they are still speaking English. But it does not follow that such rules are mere prejudice. Beliefs about correctness are themselves part of the linguistic behaviour of a community. A speaker who avoids a construction in a job application while using it freely at home is not confused; she is responding accurately to a social fact, namely that certain readers will judge her by it. A descriptive grammar that ignored such judgements would be describing an imaginary community. What the prescriptivist gets wrong is not the existence of the rules but their source. The traditional defence appeals to logic, or to the example of Latin, or to a clarity the condemned construction supposedly lacks. These appeals rarely survive inspection. The objection to splitting an infinitive, for instance, makes some sense in a language where the infinitive is a single word and cannot be split, and very little in one where it is two. The real authority of such a rule is conventional: it binds because enough educated readers expect it to be observed, and for no deeper reason. Seeing the rules as conventions of a register, rather than as laws or as prejudices, changes the question we should ask about them. It is no longer whether a usage is correct in some absolute sense, but whether a given convention earns its keep: whether it marks a distinction readers find useful, or merely sets a test that excludes those who were never taught it. Some conventions pass that test; many fail it. The point is that they can be judged, and that judging them is neither the snob's work nor the scientist's alone.
R08-A-03: A parent who hears a child begin a sentence in one language and finish it in another often worries that the child has learned neither properly. Teachers have voiced the same anxiety, and so, at times, have bilingual speakers themselves, who describe their own mixing with a kind of apology, as though it betrayed a laziness they ought to overcome. The assumption behind the worry is simple: a speaker who switches must be reaching for a word he does not have, and a speaker who is constantly reaching has not finished learning. The assumption is not absurd, and sometimes it is true. Anyone who has lived between two languages knows the moment when the word for a kitchen utensil, or for a form at the bank, has been acquired in one language and simply not in the other. But careful recordings of bilingual conversation suggest that such gaps account for only part of what happens, and not the most interesting part. Switches tend to fall at points where the grammars of the two languages fit together and to avoid points where they clash, so that a sentence begun in one language and finished in another is usually well formed by the standards of both. A speaker who was merely groping for words would not be so tidy. To switch in this way, one needs to know two grammars well enough to sense, without thinking, where they can be joined. Nor is the timing of a switch random. Speakers move into the other language to report what someone else said, to mark a change of topic, to soften a refusal, to signal that a remark is a joke, or to draw a listener in or shut one out. A grandmother's proverb may be quoted in the language she used, not because the speaker cannot translate it, but because the translation would lose the grandmother. In such uses the switch itself carries meaning, much as a change of tone does within a single language; it is a resource that monolingual speakers lack, not a failure that they have avoided. None of this means that every setting must welcome mixing. An examination set in one language, or a document that must be read by people who know only one, may reasonably require a speaker to stay within it, and a bilingual who could not do so would indeed have a problem. The error lies in treating the ability to keep languages apart as the measure of competence, and the habit of combining them as its absence. Most bilinguals can do both. Judging them by the first alone is like judging a pianist only by whether she can play with one hand.
R08-A-04: Few arguments about words are made with more confidence than the appeal to origins. Someone uses 'decimate' to mean 'destroy most of', and a correspondent points out that the word comes from a Roman military punishment in which one soldier in ten was put to death, so that its proper sense is the loss of a tenth. Someone else describes an idea as 'nice' and is reminded that the word once meant 'foolish' or 'ignorant'. The assumption in each case is that a word's earliest meaning is its real one, and that later senses are errors which happen to have spread. The assumption cannot be applied consistently, and nobody tries. If original meanings were binding, 'nice' would still be an insult, and so would a good many words now used without a second thought; the critic who insists on the Roman sense of 'decimate' does not, as a rule, insist on the earlier senses of the other words in his own sentence. Nor is there any principled place to stop. Most words have a history that runs back past the language in which they are now used, and the 'original' sense of any word is simply the earliest one of which we happen to have records. To treat that sense as authoritative is to give a vote to speakers who have been dead for centuries and to deny one to everyone now alive. What a word means is settled, as far as anything settles it, by how the people who use it understand one another. This is not a counsel of indifference, for a shift in meaning can have a cost: if a word that once marked a fine distinction comes to be used loosely, the distinction may become harder to express, and a writer may reasonably prefer to keep it. But that is an argument about present usefulness, and it has to be made on those terms. It gains nothing from the fact that the stricter sense came first. Etymology is not thereby made worthless. The history of a word can explain an odd spelling, reveal a forgotten link between two words that now look unrelated, or show how a community's way of life left its traces in the vocabulary, and it is one of the pleasures of knowing a language well; what it cannot do is serve as a court of appeal. To know where a word came from is to know something about the past of a language; it is not to know what the word must mean today.
R08-A-05: When a language is said to be endangered, the response that attracts the most attention is documentation. Linguists record the last fluent speakers telling stories, explaining how to build a house or prepare a medicine, conjugating verbs on request; the recordings are transcribed, annotated and deposited in archives designed to outlast the people who made them. Such projects are routinely described as saving the language, and the phrase is meant sincerely. Something irreplaceable is, after all, being kept from disappearing. But what is kept is not quite a language. A language, in the sense that matters to its speakers, is a practice: it is what people do when they greet one another, quarrel, court and console, and its existence consists in the fact that children acquire it from those around them. An archive holds evidence of that practice, often superb evidence, but it no longer holds the practice itself. To say that a recorded language has been saved is a little like saying that a photographed forest has been conserved. The photographs may be invaluable to someone who later tries to replant; they are not the trees. The distinction would be pedantic if it did not affect what gets done. It does. Documentation produces outputs that funders and universities know how to count: hours of recording, entries in a dictionary, a published grammar. Supporting transmission produces almost nothing of the kind. It means paying for a language nest in which grandparents look after toddlers, defending a family's decision to speak the home language against the advice of a doctor or a teacher, or making it possible for young adults to earn a living without moving to a city where the language is of no use to them. These efforts are slow, uncertain and hard to evaluate, and when resources are short, the countable work tends to win. None of this is an argument against archives. Where a community later sets out to bring back a language that has ceased to be spoken at home, the quality of the earlier documentation can decide how much of it can be recovered, and descendants have had reason to be grateful for the patience of a recorder who wrote down what their grandparents' generation did not pass on. The mistake is to treat documentation as the rescue rather than as insurance against the rescue failing. Where speakers still exist and children could still learn from them, the record is the second-best outcome, and a policy that spends most of its effort on it has quietly accepted defeat.
R08-A-06: Few natural experiments in linguistics are cited as often as the birth of a new sign language. Where deaf people who have had no shared language are brought together, at a newly founded school, say, or in a village where hereditary deafness is common, they do not remain without one for long. A system of signs takes shape among them, and within a few decades it has acquired the apparatus of a full language: consistent word order, ways of marking who did what to whom, devices for referring back to something already mentioned. The case is regularly offered as decisive evidence that the capacity for grammar is built into the human mind and needs only an occasion to express itself. The evidence is real, but it supports a more interesting conclusion than the one usually drawn from it. A deaf child raised among hearing people who do not sign will typically invent gestures to communicate with her family, and these home signs show some structure of their own: distinct gestures for actions and for things, and a tendency to place them in a regular order. What they do not become, however long the child uses them, is a full language. The leap appears only where there are many signers, and it appears in stages. The first cohort, who created the system as adolescents or adults, typically use it with more variation and less regularity than the children who learn it from them; and it is those children, receiving a still untidy system and reproducing it more consistently than they found it, who drive it towards full grammatical form. If grammar were simply waiting inside each mind for an occasion, the solitary home signer would have occasion enough. She has a lifetime of need, a willing family and an intact brain. What she lacks is other people who share her system and, above all, a younger generation to learn it from her. The emergence of a sign language thus looks less like the unveiling of a finished structure than like a process distributed across minds and generations, in which individual predispositions are amplified by repeated transmission until regularities that were faint in any single user become fixed in the community. This is not to deny that the mind brings a great deal to the task. The speed of the process, a matter of decades rather than centuries, and the resemblance between the regularities that emerge and those found in long-established languages both point to strong biases in how children learn. But the case tells against the picture of language as an organ that grows in isolation, as surely as it tells against the picture of language as a mere convention on which people agree. A language turns out to need both a particular kind of learner and a particular kind of crowd.
R08-A-07: It has become a commonplace that the metaphors buried in ordinary speech reveal the structure of ordinary thought. We speak of arguments as if they were battles, defending positions, attacking weak points, winning or losing; we speak of time as if it were space, with deadlines approaching, holidays behind us and the future ahead. On the view that has made this observation famous, such expressions are not decorations added to a literal meaning but the surface of deep conceptual mappings, in which one domain of experience is understood in terms of another. We do not merely talk about argument as war; to a large extent, it is claimed, we think about it that way, and we would argue differently if our language had taught us to think of it as, say, a dance. The opposing view is equally simple. Most of these expressions, it holds, are dead metaphors, idioms whose figurative origin is no longer felt by anyone who uses them. A speaker who says that a table has legs is not thereby thinking of the table as an animal, and a speaker who defends a position need not have soldiers anywhere in mind. On this account, inferring a mental mapping from a pattern of idioms is like inferring a belief in sorcery from the fact that people say 'bless you' after a sneeze: the history of an expression is mistaken for its present psychology. Each view, I think, gets one thing right and one thing wrong. The sceptic is right that the evidence most often cited for the mapping view is weaker than it looks. If the existence of the mapping is inferred from the expressions, and the expressions are then explained by the mapping, the argument has gone round in a circle; the sheer number of warlike expressions for argument cannot by itself show that anything in the mind corresponds to them. But the sceptic is wrong to treat these expressions as a collection of fossils. Dead metaphors are inert: one cannot extend the legs of a table into talk of its knees or its gait and expect to be understood. The metaphors of argument and time are not inert in this way. A speaker who says that her opponent's case was all ammunition and no target, or that next week is already breathing down our necks, may be using a phrase she has never heard, and she is understood at once. Something is generating these extensions, and a list of frozen idioms cannot be it. Productivity, then, rather than frequency, is the better test of whether a metaphor is alive, and by that test many everyday metaphors are alive, at least in the sense that speakers can use them as patterns for making and understanding new expressions. That is a real result, and it is more than the sceptic allows. It is also less than the mapping view claims. To show that a pattern is available for making expressions is not to show that it governs how people reason when they are not speaking, still less that a different language would leave them reasoning differently. Those further claims are empirical, and they can be settled only by evidence that does not itself consist of the very expressions in question: by watching how people solve problems, judge situations or remember events, and asking whether the metaphor leaves its mark there. The debate has often been conducted as though one had to choose between seeing language as a window onto thought and seeing it as a heap of dead habits. The more modest position is less exciting but easier to defend: our metaphors are living tools of expression, and their influence on thought beyond expression is an open question that the metaphors themselves cannot answer.
R08-A-08: Ask most people how to tell a language from a dialect and they will offer a test that sounds admirably objective: if two groups of speakers can understand each other, they speak dialects of one language; if they cannot, they speak different languages. The test has the appeal of turning a question that looks political into one that looks empirical. One need only sit speakers down together, the thought goes, and see whether conversation succeeds. The test promises, moreover, to spare the linguist from taking sides in quarrels that are seldom really about grammar. Unfortunately the test does not deliver what it promises, and the reasons are instructive. Intelligibility is a matter of degree, not of yes or no; it varies with the topic, the speed of speech and the listener's experience; and it is frequently lopsided, so that speakers of one variety follow their neighbours more easily than their neighbours follow them. Worse, it is not transitive. Across many regions, a traveller passing from village to village finds that each community understands the next without difficulty, while communities at the two ends of the chain cannot understand each other at all. Where on such a chain does one language stop and the next begin? Intelligibility alone gives no answer, and the boundaries actually drawn on maps tend to coincide with something else entirely: the borders of states, the reach of a written standard, the language of schooling and broadcasting. Everyday usage of the two words confirms this. The Scandinavian languages are counted as several, though their speakers can often converse, each using their own; the spoken varieties of Chinese are commonly called dialects, though many of them are no more mutually intelligible than languages that everyone agrees are distinct. In each case the label tracks not the distance between the varieties but the presence or absence of a shared written form, a shared state, a shared sense of belonging together. A dialect, in ordinary usage, is very often simply a variety that lacks the institutions which would have entitled it to be called a language. It is tempting to conclude that the distinction is therefore empty, a piece of politics dressed up as science, and some writers have drawn exactly that conclusion. It does not follow. That a boundary is drawn by institutions rather than by sound systems does not make it unreal, any more than the border between two countries is unreal because no river marks it. Whether a variety has a standard spelling, a literature, a place in the classroom and a name its speakers use with pride makes a large difference to how it is learned, how it changes and whether it survives. A variety used in schools and courts acquires words for law and science; one confined to the kitchen and the field tends to borrow such words, or to give way to a variety that has them. Those are facts about the social life of a variety, not about its grammar, but they are facts. The mistake, then, lies not in drawing the distinction but in where we locate it. The difference between a language and a dialect is not a property of the speech itself, waiting to be measured; it is a property of the arrangements a society has made around that speech. To see this is not to abandon the distinction. It is to understand that when a community campaigns to have its dialect recognised as a language, it is asking not for a correction of the linguistic facts but for a change in those arrangements, and that the request should be judged on those terms.
